blocks.text: The anatomical snuff box is a triangular depression located on the radial aspect of the dorsum (back) of the hand. It is formed by the tendons of the extensor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis muscles. Fractures within the anatomical snuff box are commonly associated with falls onto an outstretched hand, particularly with the wrist extended. The most fractured bone in this region is the scaphoid bone, also known as the navicular bone.
Anatomical snuff box/Radial fossa: Triangular hollow visible on the lateral aspect of the wrist when the thumb is fully extended.
Boundaries:

items.text: **Anterolateral:** Extensor pollicis brevis, Abductor pollicis longus
**Posteromedial:** Extensor pollicis longus
**Roof:** Dorsal cutaneous branch of radial nerve: Found in the skin and subcutaneous tissue of anatomical snuff box.

blocks.text: Cephalic vein: Arises from dorsal venous network of hand and crosses anatomical snuff box to travel to the anterolateral aspect of forearm.
Contents
**Radial Artery:** Crosses the floor of the anatomical snuff box.
Tenderness in the anatomical snuff box following a fall on an outstretched hand strongly suggests a scaphoid fracture, as the scaphoid bone lies in the floor of the anatomical snuff box.
This type of fracture is common and can have complications due to poor blood supply.
**Lunar (lunate) bone (Option B):** The lunate bone, found in the wrist joint, rarely fractures in injuries to the anatomical snuff box and isn't usually part of its formation.
**Cuboid bone (Option C):** The cuboid bone is one of the tarsal bones located in the foot. It is not related to the anatomical snuff box or the wrist region.
**Trapezius (Option D):** The trapezius is a large muscle located in the upper back and neck area. It is not a bone and is not related to the anatomical snuff box or wrist injuries.
The axillary nerve (C5-C6) is vulnerable to injury during intramuscular injections in the deltoid muscle, especially if injected too low or too deep.
Injury results in:

items.text: Flattening of the shoulder (loss of deltoid muscle bulk).
Loss of shoulder contour (due to deltoid atrophy).
Weakness in abduction beyond 15° (deltoid function loss).
Sensory loss over the lateral shoulder (regimental badge area).

blocks.text: Prevention: Intramuscular injections should be given in the upper lateral quadrant of the deltoid to avoid axillary nerve injury.

blocks.title: Axillary Nerve Injury
rows: Arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus (C5-C6).
Passes through quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery.
Deltoid muscle (shoulder abduction) and teres minor (external rotation).
Skin over the lateral shoulder (regimental badge area) via the superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm.
Improper intramuscular injection, shoulder dislocation, humeral surgical neck fracture.
Shoulder atrophy, loss of contour, weakness in abduction, and sensory loss over the deltoid region.

blocks.text: **Rotator cuff (Option A):** Incorrect: Involved in shoulder stability but does not cause loss of shoulder contour when injured.
**Posterior circumflex artery (Option B):** Incorrect: Runs with the axillary nerve but its injury would cause vascular compromise, not motor weakness.
**Lateral cutaneous nerve of arm (Option C):** Incorrect: Only provides sensory innervation; it does not affect shoulder shape or movement.

A positive Trendelenburg test indicates weakness of the hip abductors, specifically the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus. These muscles are innervated by the superior gluteal nerve. In this case, the right-sided Trendelenburg sign means the right gluteus medius and minimus are weak, which occurs due to damage to the right superior gluteal nerve.

Trendelenberg sign: When the body's weight is balanced on one leg, the gluteal muscles on the supported side help elevate the opposite, unsupported side of the pelvis. However, if there is a malfunction in the abductor mechanism, the Sound side sinks, which is referred to as a positive Trendelenburg sign (uncompensated).

This sign indicates issues with hip abductors, such as paralysis of the gluteus medius and minimus; problems with the fulcrum, including congenital or pathological hip dislocations; and concerns related to body weight, such as an unhealed fracture of the femoral neck.

When patients with the gluteus medius and minimus paralysis walk, they have a characteristic lurching gait ie, during the single leg supporting phase of walking, there is leaning of the trunk to the affected side known as the compensated Trendelenburg sign. Duck waddling gait is seen when both the sides are affected.

items.text: **Right inferior gluteal nerve (option A):** The inferior gluteal nerve innervates the gluteus maximus, which is responsible for hip extension, not abduction. Damage here would cause difficulty rising from a seated position or climbing stairs, not a Trendelenburg sign.
**Left superior gluteal nerve (option C):** If the left superior gluteal nerve were affected, the right hip would drop when standing on the left leg, not the right leg.
**Left inferior gluteal nerve (option D):** The inferior gluteal nerve does not control hip abduction, and the left-sided nerve would not cause a right-sided Trendelenburg sign.

blocks.text: The 1st lumbrical is primarily innervated by the median nerve. The first lumbrical is located in the hand, and it helps in flexing the metacarpophalangeal joint and extending the interphalangeal joints. It is innervated by the median nerve, which supplies the lumbricals 1 and 2 (the first two lumbricals).

The median nerve, which innervates the muscles responsible for thumb abduction and opposition, is formed from the anterior rami of spinal nerves C5 to T1, derived from the brachial plexus. It primarily supplies the anterior forearm muscles and the t henar eminence of the hand, which includes:
Muscles of the Thenar eminence:

items.text: **Abductor Pollicis Brevis:** Responsible for thumb abduction.
**Flexor Pollicis Brevis:** Assists in thumb flexion.
**Opponens Pollicis:** Enables opposition of the thumb.

blocks.text: **Lumbricals (Lateral 2):** Responsible for flexion at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and extension at the interphalangeal (IP) joints of the 2nd and 3rd digits
**Sensory supply:** Lateral 3 1⁄2 digits in the palmar aspect & tip of same digits on the dorsum..
Brachial Plexus
The brachial plexus is a network of nerves formed by the anterior rami of the lower four cervical nerves (C5, C6, C7, C8) and the first thoracic nerve (T1)
Components of the Brachial Plexus:

items.text: **Roots:** Five roots (C5 to T1), deep to the scalenus anterior muscle.
**Trunks:** Upper trunk: C5 and C6, Middle trunk: C7, Lower trunk: C8 and T1
**Divisions:** Located behind the clavicle.
**Cords:** Three cords form from the divisions
**Lateral cord:** Anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks.
**Medial cord:** Anterior division of the lower trunk.
**Posterior cord:** Posterior divisions of all three trunks.

blocks.text: Branches:

items.text: **From Roots**
Long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7)
Dorsal scapular nerve (C5)
**From Trunks**
Suprascapular nerve (C5, C6)
Nerve to subclavius (C5, C6)
**Lateral Cord**
Lateral pectoral nerve (C5, C6, C7)
Lateral root of median nerve (C5, C6, C7)
Musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6, C7)
**Medial Cord**
Medial pectoral nerve (C8, T1)
Medial cutaneous nerve of arm (C8, T1)
Medial cutaneous nerve of forearm (C8, T1)
Medial root of median nerve (C8, T1)
Ulnar nerve (C7, C8, T1)
**Posterior Cord**
Radial nerve (C5, C6, C7, C8, T1)
Axillary nerve (C5, C6)
Thoraco-dorsal nerve (C6, C7, C8)
Upper subscapular nerve (C5, C6)
Lower subscapular nerve (C5, C6)

blocks.text: **Radial nerve (option A):** The radial nerve innervates the extensor muscles of the forearm and hand, not the lumbricals, which are responsible for flexion and extension of the fingers.

items.text: **Ulnar nerve (option C):** The ulnar nerve innervates the lumbricals 3 and 4 (the last two lumbricals), not the first lumbrical.
**Musculocutaneous nerve (option D):** The musculocutaneous nerve primarily innervates the flexor muscles of the upper arm (e.g., biceps brachii), not the lumbricals of the hand.

blocks.text: The image shows "claw hand deformity", which is characteristic of ulnar nerve injury. The deformity results from paralysis of the lumbricals (which flex the MCP joints and extend the IP joints of the 4th and 5th fingers). The 4th and 5th fingers are hyperextended at the MCP joints and flexed at the IP joints, leading to a claw-like appearance.
Common causes in leprosy: Ulnar nerve involvement due to nerve infiltration and fibrosis, leading to motor impairment.

blocks.title: Ulnar Nerve Palsy and Claw Hand
rows: MCP hyperextension, IP flexion (mainly in 4th & 5th fingers)
Leprosy, trauma at the elbow (cubital tunnel) or wrist (Guyon's canal)
Physiotherapy, nerve grafting, claw correction surgery

blocks.text: Radial nerve (Option B): Incorrect because its injury causes wrist drop, not claw hand.
**Median nerve (Option C):** Incorrect because it causes ape hand deformity (loss of thumb opposition).
**Posterior interosseous nerve (Option D):** Incorrect because it affects finger extension, leading to finger drop, not claw hand.

Klumpke's paralysis occurs due to injury of the lower brachial plexus (C8-T1), which affects the intrinsic muscles of the hand, particularly the lumbricals, interossei, and thenar/hypothenar muscles. This results in "claw hand", where there is hyperextension of the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion of the interphalangeal joints, leading to a characteristic clawed appearance of the fingers.

blocks.title: Klumpke’s Paralysis
rows: Lower trunk of the brachial plexus

Undue arm abduction (e.g., clutching after a fall)
Birth injury

Intrinsic muscles of the hand (T1)
Ulnar flexors of the wrist and fingers (C8)

Claw hand: unopposed action of long flexors and extensors
Hyperextension at metacarpophalangeal joints
Flexion at interphalangeal joints

Complete claw hand
Cutaneous anesthesia and analgesia along the ulnar border of forearm and hand
Horner’s Syndrome (if T1 injured near sympathetic ganglion)
Symptoms: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis, enophthalmos, loss of ciliospinal reflex
Warmer, drier skin in the sensory loss area due to arteriolar dilation and lack of sweating
Long-term paralysis results in dry, scaly skin, brittle nails, and atrophy of finger pulp

blocks.text: Horner’s syndrome is also associated with lower brachial plexus injuries but is not the primary clinical finding.

items.text: **Policeman tip hand (option A):** This is a sign of upper brachial plexus injury (C5-C6), typically resulting in waiter's tip position due to paralysis of the deltoid, biceps, and brachioradialis.
**Wrist drop (option B):** This is a feature of radial nerve injury, leading to the inability to extend the wrist and fingers. It is not a characteristic finding in Klumpke’s paralysis.

**Horner’s syndrome (option D)** can occur in lower brachial plexus injury due to sympathetic fiber disruption, leading to ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis on the same side. While present, it is not the primary clinical feature of Klumpke's paralysis.

blocks.text: The flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) is responsible for flexion at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of the medial four fingers. If the FDP to the ring finger is injured, the patient will be unable to fully flex the ring finger when making a fist.
Muscles Involved in the Movement of Interphalangeal Joints
The interphalangeal (IP) joints include:

items.text: Proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints – between proximal and middle phalanges.
Distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints – between middle and distal phalanges.

Lateral part (index & middle fingers): Median nerve
Medial part (ring & little fingers): Ulnar nerve

Extensor digitorum
Extensor indicis (index finger only)
Extensor digiti minimi (little finger only)
Assists in extension of PIP & DIP joints

Lumbricals: Lateral 2 (median nerve), medial 2 (ulnar nerve)

blocks.text: Median nerve (Option A): Incorrect because median nerve injury would affect multiple fingers (thumb, index, middle), not just the ring finger alone.
**Flexor retinaculum (Option B):** Incorrect because injury to the retinaculum leads to carpal tunnel syndrome, affecting the median nerve distribution, not isolated finger flexion.
**Flexor pollicis longus (Option D):** Incorrect because this muscle only flexes the thumb, not the ring finger.
The biceps brachii is the primary mover (agonist) for forearm flexion at the elbow joint. When lifting the forearm, it contracts to generate movement by pulling the radius upward.

blocks.title: Muscle Roles in Movement
rows: Muscle that opposes the primary mover.
Triceps brachii extends the elbow, opposing the biceps.
Assists the primary mover by adding force or stability.
Brachialis helps the biceps in flexion.
Stabilizes the origin of the primary mover.
Rotator cuff muscles stabilize the shoulder joint during flexion.

blocks.text: **Synergistic (Option A):** Incorrect because the brachialis acts as a synergist, not the biceps brachii.
**Fixator (Option B):** Incorrect because fixators stabilize joints, like the rotator cuff stabilizing the shoulder.
**Antagonist (Option C):** Incorrect because the triceps brachii is the antagonist, opposing biceps action.

The distal end of the ulna does not directly participate in the formation of the wrist joint. Instead, it forms the ulnar styloid process, which provides attachment for ligaments and provides stability to the wrist joint. The ulna primarily articulates with the radius at the distal radioulnar joint, which is separate from the wrist joint itself.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option A: Scaphoid:** The scaphoid bone, a carpal bone of the wrist, articulates with the distal radius, crucial for wrist joint formation.
**Option B: Triquetrum:** The triquetrum is another carpal bone that participates in the formation of the wrist joint. It articulates with the distal end of the ulna and the lunate bone.
**Option C: Distal end of radius:** The radial articular surface at the end of the radius is vital for the wrist joint, connecting with carpal bones like the scaphoid and lunate.

blocks.text: Loss of flexion at the interphalangeal joint of the thumb after a supracondylar fracture is due to anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) involvement. AIN, a branch of the median nerve in the forearm, innervates deep flexor muscles, including the flexor pollicis longus responsible for thumb flexion. With a supracondylar humerus fracture, AIN compression or injury can weaken or paralyze the flexor pollicis longus, causing thumb joint flexion inability.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option A. Deep branch of ulnar nerve:** The deep branch of the ulnar nerve innervates the hypothenar eminence and intrinsic hand muscles, not thumb interphalangeal joint flexion.
**Option B. Median nerve:** Median nerve injury typically leads to a broader pattern of motor and sensory deficits in the hand.

**Option C. Posterior interosseous nerve:** The posterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the radial nerve, mainly innervates extensor muscles in the forearm and doesn't play a direct role in thumb flexion.

blocks.text: Incorrect Option:

items.text: **Option B. Hypothenar muscles wasting:** Lesion of the median nerve wouldn't directly cause wasting or weakness of the hypothenar muscles, as they're innervated by the ulnar nerve, not the median nerve.

**Option C. Loss of sensation at the tip of the radial tubercle:** A median nerve lesion wouldn't cause loss of sensation at the radial tubercle tip, as its innervation comes from radial nerve branches, not the median nerve.

**Option D. Loss of sensation of the 4th interdigital cleft:** A median nerve lesion wouldn't lead to sensory loss in the 4th interdigital cleft since its innervation comes from the ulnar nerve, not the median nerve.

blocks.text: The axillary nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin overlying the posterior border of the deltoid muscle and extends down to cover the long head of the triceps muscle.
Incorrect options:

items.text: **Option A. Musculocutaneous nerve:** This nerve supplies motor innervation to the anterior compartment muscles of the arm and does not supply the mentioned sensory area.
**Option B. Radial nerve:** The radial nerve supplies sensory innervation to the posterior aspect of the arm but does not specifically provide innervation to the mentioned area.
**Option C. Ulnar nerve:** The ulnar nerve primarily supplies sensory innervation to the medial aspect of the hand and does not innervate the mentioned area.

blocks.text: The middle finger has two dorsal interossei muscles. The dorsal interossei muscles are a group of muscles located in the hand between the metacarpal bones. They play a role in finger abduction, which is the movement of the fingers away from the midline of the hand. The middle finger is the only finger that has two dorsal interossei muscles.
Incorrect Option:

items.text: **Option A:** The index finger has only one dorsal interosseous muscle.
**Option B:** The little finger, also known as the Pinky finger, has only one dorsal interosseous muscle.
**Option D:** The ring finger has only one dorsal interosseous muscle.

blocks.text: The lumbrical muscles, marked as A in the image, play a role in flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joint.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option B. Extension:** Extension straightens or widens the angle between bones. Lumbrical muscles don't aid in extending the metacarpophalangeal joint.
**Option C. Adduction:** In the metacarpophalangeal joint, adduction brings fingers closer together. Lumbrical muscles aren't involved in adduction.
**Option D. Abduction:** At the metacarpophalangeal joint, abduction spreads fingers apart. Lumbrical muscles aren't involved in abduction.

blocks.text: This statement is correct. De Quervain's tenosynovitis specifically affects the tendons of the abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB). These tendons run along the thumb side of the wrist and are responsible for thumb movement
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option A: Fingers are held in mild extension:** This is incorrect. In De Quervain's tenosynovitis, the affected fingers are typically flexed, not extended.

**Option C: Most common involvement is index finger:** This is incorrect. De Quervain's tenosynovitis mainly affects the thumb side of the wrist, involving the tendons of APL and EPB, and doesn't usually involve the index finger.
**Option D: Treatment is surgery:** This is incorrect. Surgery isn't usually the first treatment for De Quervain's tenosynovitis.

blocks.text: Initially, conservative measures like rest, splinting, anti-inflammatory medication, and physical therapy are attempted.

The radial nerve supplies the area marked by the arrow in the image, which corresponds to the anatomical snuff box. The anatomical snuff box is located on the dorsum (back) of the hand and is formed by tendons of the extensor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis muscles. The radial nerve provides sensory innervation to this area.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option B: Posterior interosseous nerve:** The posterior interosseous nerve is a branch of the radial nerve that supplies the deep extensor muscles of the forearm. It does not directly innervate the area marked in the image.

**Option C: Median nerve:** The median nerve primarily supplies the palmar aspect of the hand, including the thenar muscles and lateral 3 and a half digits. It does not directly supply the area marked in the image.

**Option D: Ulnar nerve:** The ulnar nerve primarily innervates the medial aspect of the hand, including the hypothenar muscles and the ulnar side of the palm. It does not directly supply the area marked in the image.

blocks.text: The median nerve is the correct answer. It provides motor innervation to the lumbrical muscles of the hand, including the 2nd lumbrical. The lumbrical muscles are responsible for flexing the metacarpophalangeal joints and extending the interphalangeal joints of the fingers.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option A: Posterior interosseous nerve:** The posterior interosseous nerve primarily supplies the extensor muscles of the forearm. It does not supply the structure marked in the image, which is the 2nd lumbrical.
**Option C: Anterior interosseous nerve:** The anterior interosseous nerve supplies the deep flexor muscles of the forearm, but it does not directly innervate the lumbrical muscles.

**Option D: Ulnar nerve:** The ulnar nerve innervates the muscles of the hypothenar eminence, interosseous muscles, and intrinsic muscles of the hand. It does not directly supply the 2nd lumbrical muscle.

blocks.text: The image shows the extensor carpi radialis muscle, which is indicated by the arrow. This muscle is located in the forearm and plays a role in extending and abducting the wrist.
Incorrect options:

items.text: **Option B: Brachioradialis:** The arrow in the image doesn't point to the brachioradialis muscle, which is located in the forearm but positioned more laterally compared to the extensor carpi radialis.
**Option C: Supinator:** The arrow in the image doesn't point to the supinator muscle, situated in the forearm, assisting in forearm supination by rotating the palm upward.

**Option D: Flexor carpi radialis brevis:** The arrow in the image doesn't indicate the flexor carpi radialis, a muscle responsible for wrist flexion.radialis brevis." The correct name for the muscle associated with flexing the wrist is the flexor carpi radialis, but it is not indicated by the arrow in the image.

blocks.text: The symptoms described, hypothenar muscle wasting and loss of sensation of the medial one and a half digits, indicate the involvement of the ulnar nerve. The ulnar nerve is responsible for the innervation of the hypothenar muscles (located in the palm of the hand) and provides sensory innervation to the medial one and a half digits (the little finger and half of the ring finger).
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option A. Musculocutaneous:** The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior arm muscles but not the hypothenar muscles or sensation to the described digits.
**Option B. Radial:** The radial nerve innervates the extensor muscles of the arm and forearm and does not supply the hypothenar muscles or provide sensory innervation to the described digits.

**Option D. Median:** The median nerve supplies the muscles of the anterior compartment of the forearm and does not innervate the hypothenar muscles or provide sensory innervation to the described digits.

blocks.text: Injuries to the anatomical snuffbox can lead to fractures of the scaphoid bone, which is one of the carpal bones located in the wrist. The scaphoid bone is vulnerable to fractures due to its location and shape. Fractures of the scaphoid bone can result from a fall onto an outstretched hand, particularly when the force is transmitted through the thumb.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option A. Lunate:** The lunate is another carpal bone, but it is not directly associated with the anatomical snuffbox.
**Option C. Hamate:** The hamate is a carpal bone located on the ulnar side of the wrist and is not directly associated with the anatomical snuffbox.
**Option D. Trapezium:** The trapezium is a carpal bone located at the base of the thumb, but it is not part of the anatomical snuffbox
